cold.title: Write it your way
cold.goal: Write a prompt in your own words, run it once, and keep the answer as your starting point.
why: Your first answer shows what happens when you ask the way you usually ask. You can only see what a better prompt adds by comparing it with where you started.
You run it once and keep whatever comes back. A second try would replace the very thing you want to look at.
This course runs your AI in a folder that holds only your prompt, so the answer depends only on what the prompt says. This is this course's way of working. Other approaches work too.
Your AI runs on an everyday model, and the app records which one. You use the same model for the next run, because a fair comparison changes one thing at a time.
instructions: Read the scenario and the rough notes below. The five things in the list are in your head, not in the notes.

Write a prompt in your own words that asks for the end-of-week update. There is no right way to do it, and there are no hints here. You do not need to paste the notes, because the app adds them under your words.

Press Save my prompt. The first time you save, your AI window starts by itself. It is a new chat on the model chosen with the Sonnet / Haiku switch above it (Sonnet unless you changed it), and the app records that model for you. Sonnet is the everyday default and Haiku is the lighter, faster one. The most capable flagship models, such as Opus, are not offered, because this course compares prompts, not models. A change to the switch applies the next time your AI starts. Each step opens a new chat, so nothing from an earlier step carries over.
Wait until your AI window is ready for you to type.
Press Copy under Text to paste. Click in the AI window, paste with {paste_key} and press Enter. Do not add anything.
Your AI saves its answer in a file called output.txt. The app saves it as your answer, closes your AI window and finishes this step. Then press Continue.
cold.instruction: Save only your answer to output.txt. Do nothing else.
cold.folder_label: Folder with only your prompt and the rough notes

scenario.intro: It is Friday afternoon and you need to send your project lead a short end-of-week update. You will use your AI tool to turn your rough notes into the update.

requirements.label: It is sent as a Teams message, not an email
The work is grouped by client (Northwind, Contoso, Internal), not by day
It calls out the blocker and what you need to resolve it
The tone is factual, not self-promotional

scenario.task: Your task: write a prompt in your own words that asks for the end-of-week update. Run it once and keep the answer.

troubleshooting.problem: Your AI asks you a question before it writes the update.
troubleshooting.fix: Reply in the AI window: go ahead with your best guess. That keeps this a single run.

troubleshooting.problem: Your AI reports a temporary error, such as a busy service or a network problem.
troubleshooting.fix: Wait a moment and ask it again in the AI window. If it keeps failing, press Stop, then Open a new AI chat, and paste the text again.

troubleshooting.problem: Nothing happens after you paste the text.
troubleshooting.fix: Look at the AI window. If your AI is set to ask for approval, it may be waiting for you. Answer it there.
The app needs a file called output.txt with text in it. If your AI printed the answer but saved nothing, press Open a new AI chat, copy the text again and paste it.

troubleshooting.problem: You changed your prompt after your AI window opened.
troubleshooting.fix: Press Save my prompt, copy the text again and paste it into the same AI window. The window keeps running, and the text to paste always shows your latest saved prompt.

troubleshooting.problem: Your AI window did not open when you saved.
troubleshooting.fix: Press Open a new AI chat. If it still will not start, open Settings, go to the Setup group and check the command. Type the same command in a normal terminal to confirm that it works.

score.title: Score what you got
score.goal: Check the answer against the five things you knew, and name one thing it missed.
why: A score gives you something to compare against. Without one, a second answer is only a different answer.
You are the judge here. There is no answer key, and the app does not read the answer to decide for you.
Counting how many of the five were met is quick, and it needs no technical skill.
instructions: Read the answer on the page next to the five things you knew.
For each of the five, choose Yes if the answer did it and No if it did not.
Write one thing the answer got wrong or missed.
Say whether that was in your prompt: Yes, No or Not sure.
When the list of what is still missing is empty, press Continue.

troubleshooting.problem: You are not sure whether the answer met one of the five.
troubleshooting.fix: Choose the closest answer and move on. This is your own judgment, and the app does not grade it.

troubleshooting.problem: The answer is missing or looks wrong.
troubleshooting.fix: Go back to the earlier step to look at your prompt and the answer the app saved. The answer shown here is exactly what your AI saved.

rewrite.title: Try a framework
rewrite.goal: Write the same request again with labels, run it once in a new chat, and keep the answer.
why: Labels give each category of need a place, so it is harder to leave one out.
A new chat means nothing from the first run carries over, so any difference comes from the new prompt.
You use the same rough notes and the same model as before, so only the prompt changes. This course runs your AI in a folder that holds only your prompt. Other approaches work too.
The frameworks here are samples, and you can use labels of your own. Use whichever reads clearest to you.
instructions: Choose a set of labels: RTCC, RISE or your own.
Press Insert labels to put that set in the editor, then fill in each label in your own words. You can change the labels if they do not fit.

Press Save my prompt. The first time you save, your AI window starts by itself as a new chat, so nothing from your first run carries over. Leave the Sonnet / Haiku switch as it was for your first run, so both runs use the same model. The app records it for you.
Wait until your AI window is ready for you to type.
Press Copy under Text to paste. Click in the AI window, paste with {paste_key} and press Enter.
Your AI saves its answer in a file called output.txt. The app saves it as your answer, closes your AI window and finishes this step when everything above is in place. Then press Continue.

labels.description: Four labels: Role, Task, Context and Constraints. Fill in each in your own words.

Role: who the AI acts as

Context: the background it needs
Constraints: limits and format

Expectation: what a good result looks like

rescore.title: Score it again
rescore.goal: Score the second answer on the same five things, then compare your two runs.
why: The same five things make the two scores fair to compare.
Putting both runs side by side shows what the labels changed, and what they did not.
One run each is a quick look, not proof. It cannot show how much answers vary from one try to the next.
instructions: Read the second answer next to the five things you knew.
For each of the five, choose Yes if the answer did it and No if it did not.
Look at your two runs side by side.
Write what your labels made you add, and what made the second answer better. If it was not better, write which part of the prompt is still missing.
When the list of what is still missing is empty, press Continue.

reflections.label: What did your labels make you add?

own.title: Use it on your own work
own.goal: Rewrite one real prompt from your own work with labels, and keep both versions.
why: The skill only sticks when you use it on work that matters to you.
Keeping the before and after side by side shows what the labels added, and the after version is ready to reuse.
No AI is run in this step. It is a writing exercise, so you can take your time.
instructions: Choose one real prompt from your own work. If you do not have one, choose a task you repeat and write the prompt you would use for it.
Leave out anything confidential. The text stays on this computer, in your project folder.
Paste or write it in the first box as it is.
Rewrite it with labels, from a framework or labels of your own, in the second box.
Say which labels you used, then press Save my work. When everything is filled in, the step finishes by itself.

troubleshooting.problem: You do not have a real prompt to use.
troubleshooting.fix: Pick a task you repeat, such as a weekly message or a summary, and write the prompt you would use today. Then rewrite it.
Replace the private parts with general words before you paste it. The text stays on this computer, but leaving the details out is safer.
